slides.narration: A torch reflector, a make-up mirror and the wide mirror on a bus all use curved mirrors. In this part we name the important points of a spherical mirror, prove that its focal length is half its radius of curvature, fix a sign convention, derive the mirror formula, and use it to predict where an image forms, how large it is, and whether it can be caught on a screen.

slides.heading: The parts of a spherical mirror
slides.body_md: A **spherical mirror** is part of a hollow sphere: **concave** if the inside is silvered, **convex** if the outside is.
bullets: **Pole P:** centre of the mirror’s surface. **Centre of curvature C:** centre of the sphere. **Radius of curvature R:** PC.
**Principal axis:** the line through P and C. **Aperture:** the width of the mirror.
**Principal focus F:** where rays parallel to the axis meet after reflection (concave), or seem to come from (convex). **Focal length f:** PF.
**Paraxial rays:** rays close and nearly parallel to the axis; all the results here assume them.

slides.narration: The pole is the middle of the mirror, the centre of curvature is the centre of the sphere it was cut from, and the distance between them is the radius of curvature. The principal axis joins them. Rays parallel to the axis meet at the principal focus of a concave mirror, or seem to spread out from it for a convex one. We always assume paraxial rays, close to the axis.

slides.heading: Why the focal length is half the radius
slides.body_md:
A ray parallel to the axis strikes the mirror at M; CM is the normal. Angle of incidence $\theta$ = angle of reflection $\theta$, and $\angle MCF = \theta$ (alternate angles). So triangle FCM is **isosceles**: $FC = FM$.
For a paraxial ray M is very close to P, so $FM \approx FP$. Then $FC = FP$: F is the **midpoint** of PC.
$$f = \dfrac{R}{2}$$
bullets: The same proof works for a convex mirror, with F behind it.
For wide rays F moves towards the mirror (spherical aberration), so only paraxial rays meet at one point.

slides.narration: Follow one ray parallel to the axis. At the mirror the normal points to the centre of curvature, and the ray reflects at the same angle theta. Because the incident ray is parallel to the axis, the angle at C is also theta, so the triangle formed by F, C and M has two equal angles and two equal sides. For a ray close to the axis, F M is nearly F P, so F sits halfway between P and C.

slides.heading: The New Cartesian sign convention
slides.body_md: ISC uses the **New Cartesian** convention, with the light drawn travelling from left to right:
bullets: All distances are measured **from the pole**.
Distances in the direction of the incident light are **positive**; against it, **negative**.
Heights above the principal axis are **positive**; below it, **negative**.
So a real object has $u < 0$; a concave mirror has $f < 0$ and a convex mirror $f > 0$; real images (in front) have $v < 0$.

slides.heading: Locating an image: four useful rays
slides.body_md: Any two of these rays from the top of the object fix the top of the image:
bullets: Where the reflected rays actually meet, the image is **real** and can be caught on a screen.
Where they only **seem** to come from (traced back behind the mirror), the image is **virtual**.

headers: Incident ray from the top of the object
rows: Passes through F (concave) or appears to come from F (convex)
Through F (or heading towards F of a convex mirror)
Through C (or heading towards C of a convex mirror)
Returns along itself (it meets the mirror normally)
Reflected at an equal angle on the other side of the axis

visual.alt: Table of the four standard rays for locating the image in a spherical mirror: parallel to the axis, through the focus, through the centre of curvature, and to the pole

slides.narration: To find an image, follow two rays from the top of the object. A ray parallel to the axis reflects through the focus. A ray through the focus comes back parallel. A ray through the centre of curvature hits the mirror head on and returns along itself. A ray to the pole reflects symmetrically about the axis. Where the reflected rays cross, there is a real image; if they only seem to cross behind the mirror, the image is virtual.

slides.heading: Deriving the mirror formula
slides.body_md:
Object AB beyond C; image A′B′. Triangles A′B′F and MDF are similar, and so are A′B′P and ABP. With $MD = AB$ and $D \approx P$:
$$\dfrac{A'B'}{AB} = \dfrac{B'F}{FP} = \dfrac{B'P}{BP}$$
Signs: $B'P = -v$, $BP = -u$, $FP = -f$, $B'F = f - v$:
$$\dfrac{f - v}{-f} = \dfrac{-v}{-u} \;\Rightarrow\; \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$$
bullets: The formula holds for concave and convex mirrors and for real and virtual images, once the signs are put in.

For a small mirror, M D equals the object height and D is at the pole, so both ratios equal the image height over the object height. Writing each length with its sign and rearranging gives one over v plus one over u equals one over f.

slides.heading: Magnification
slides.body_md:
The **linear magnification** is the ratio of image height to object height:
$$m = \dfrac{h'}{h} = -\dfrac{v}{u}$$
From the similar triangles A′B′P and ABP, with the signs of the convention.
bullets: m has no unit. A real image of a real object always has negative m; a virtual one positive m.

rows: Image real and inverted (in front of the mirror)
Image virtual and erect (behind the mirror)

visual.alt: Table of what the sign and size of the magnification tell you about an image

slides.narration: Magnification is the image height divided by the object height, and from the triangles at the pole it equals minus v over u. Its sign tells you the nature of the image. A negative magnification means a real, inverted image in front of the mirror; a positive one means a virtual, erect image behind it. Its size tells you whether the image is larger or smaller than the object.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a real, magnified image
slides.body_md: An object 3.0 cm tall stands 18 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 12 cm. Find the position, size and nature of the image.
bullets: Step 1 — signs: $u = -18$ cm, $f = -12$ cm.
Step 2 — $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{12} + \dfrac{1}{18} = -\dfrac{1}{36}$, so $v = -36$ cm (36 cm in front: **real**).
Step 3 — $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{-36}{-18} = -2$; $h' = mh = -6.0$ cm: **inverted, twice the size**.

slides.heading: Where the image forms in a concave mirror
slides.body_md: As the object moves from far away towards the mirror:
bullets: Real images move out from F to infinity while the object moves in from infinity to F.
Only an object inside F gives a virtual, erect image.

visual.alt: Table of the image formed by a concave mirror for six object positions, from infinity to inside the focus

slides.narration: A distant object gives a tiny real image at the focus. As the object comes closer, the image moves out and grows: between F and C when the object is beyond C, at C when the object is at C, and beyond C when the object is between C and F. With the object at F the image is at infinity. Inside F, the image jumps behind the mirror and becomes virtual, erect and magnified.

slides.heading: Convex mirrors
slides.body_md: For a convex mirror $f > 0$ and, for a real object, $u < 0$, so $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u}$ is the sum of two positive terms:
bullets: v is positive and **smaller than f**: the image is always **virtual**, behind the mirror, between P and F.
m = −v/u is positive and less than 1: always **erect and diminished**.
A wide region in front fits into a small image: a large **field of view**.

slides.narration: A convex mirror always behaves the same way for a real object. With a positive focal length and a negative object distance, one over v is a sum of two positive numbers, so v is positive and smaller than f. The image is virtual, behind the mirror and between the pole and the focus. It is always erect and smaller than the object, and a wide scene squeezes into a small image.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a rear-view mirror
slides.body_md: The convex rear-view mirror of a car has a radius of curvature of 80 cm. A truck 2.4 m tall is 6.0 m behind it. Find the position and height of the truck’s image.

visual.alt: Worked table: focal length plus 40 centimetres, image 37.5 centimetres behind the mirror, magnification 0.0625, image 15 centimetres tall and erect

slides.narration: Half the radius gives a focal length of plus forty centimetres. With the truck six metres away, one over v is one fortieth plus one six hundredth, giving thirty seven and a half centimetres behind the mirror. The magnification is about six hundredths, so the truck appears only fifteen centimetres tall: smaller, and so seemingly farther away, than it really is.

slides.heading: Uses of spherical mirrors
slides.body_md: Each use follows from where the object or source sits:
bullets: Convex mirrors make vehicles look smaller, hence farther away, than they are: drivers are warned that objects are closer than they appear.

rows: Lamp at F gives a parallel beam
Face inside F: erect, magnified image
Erect image, wide field of view
Large area seen in a small mirror

visual.alt: Table of uses of concave and convex mirrors with the reason for each

slides.narration: A lamp at the focus of a concave reflector sends out a parallel beam, as in a torch or headlight. Hold your face inside the focus of a concave mirror and you see an enlarged, upright image, which is why shaving and make-up mirrors are concave. Large concave mirrors concentrate sunlight. Convex mirrors give an erect, wide view, so they are used on vehicles, in shops and at sharp bends in hill roads.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: From P; along the light +; real object $u < 0$; concave $f < 0$, convex $f > 0$
Real images unless the object is inside F
Always virtual, erect, diminished, between P and F

visual.alt: Summary table of the focal length, the sign convention, the mirror formula, magnification, and the images of concave and convex mirrors

slides.narration: To sum up: for rays near the axis, the focal length is half the radius of curvature. Measure distances from the pole, positive along the light, so real objects have negative u and concave mirrors negative f. The mirror formula is one over v plus one over u equals one over f, and the magnification is minus v over u. Concave mirrors give real images except inside F; convex mirrors always give small, erect, virtual images.

slides.narration: A pool looks shallower than it is, a glass slab shifts what you see through it sideways, and a hair-thin glass fibre carries internet data under the ocean. All of these come from refraction at flat surfaces. In this part we state Snell’s law, link refractive indices across several media, measure apparent depth, and see how light can be trapped completely by total internal reflection.

slides.heading: Refraction and Snell’s law
slides.body_md:
When light crosses from one medium into another it changes speed and, unless it meets the boundary normally, its direction.
**Laws of refraction:** (1) the incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal lie in one plane; (2) **Snell’s law:**
$$n_1\sin i = n_2\sin r \qquad\text{or}\qquad \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = {}_1n_2$$
bullets: Absolute refractive index $n = c/v$: the speed in vacuum over the speed in the medium.
Into a denser medium (larger n) the ray bends **towards** the normal; into a rarer one, **away** from it.
Frequency does not change; speed and wavelength fall by the factor n.

slides.narration: Light slows down in glass, and a ray meeting the glass at an angle bends. Snell’s law says n one times the sine of the angle of incidence equals n two times the sine of the angle of refraction. The absolute refractive index is the speed of light in vacuum divided by its speed in the medium. Entering a denser medium the ray bends towards the normal. The frequency stays fixed, so the wavelength shrinks.

slides.heading: Relative refractive index
slides.body_md:
The refractive index of medium 2 **relative to** medium 1:
$${}_1n_2 = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \dfrac{v_1}{v_2}$$
bullets: Reversibility: ${}_2n_1 = \dfrac{1}{{}_1n_2}$ (a ray retraces its path).

visual.alt: Table of refractive indices of air, water, crown glass and diamond with the speed of light in each, equal to c divided by n

slides.narration: The refractive index of a second medium relative to the first is the sine of the incidence angle over the sine of the refraction angle, and it equals the ratio of their absolute indices, or the inverse ratio of the speeds. Because light retraces its path, the index of medium one relative to medium two is just the reciprocal. Glass relative to water, for example, is one point five over one point three three.

slides.heading: Several parallel media: ₁n₂ × ₂n₃ × ₃n₁ = 1
slides.body_md:
A ray passes from medium 1 through parallel layers 2 and 3 and back into medium 1. At each boundary $n\sin\theta$ is unchanged, so it leaves at its original angle. Applying Snell’s law at each face:
$${}_1n_2\;{}_2n_3\;{}_3n_1 = \dfrac{\sin\theta_1}{\sin\theta_2}\cdot\dfrac{\sin\theta_2}{\sin\theta_3}\cdot\dfrac{\sin\theta_3}{\sin\theta_1} = 1$$
bullets: Hence ${}_2n_3 = \dfrac{{}_1n_3}{{}_1n_2}$: relative indices follow from absolute ones.
The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray because the first and last media are the same.

slides.heading: A parallel-sided slab: lateral shift
slides.body_md:
At the first face $\sin i = n\sin r$; at the second, $n\sin r = \sin e$. So $e = i$: the emergent ray is **parallel** to the incident ray but displaced sideways by the **lateral shift**
$$d = \dfrac{t\,\sin(i - r)}{\cos r}$$
bullets: The path inside the slab has length $t/\cos r$; d is that length times $\sin(i - r)$.
d = 0 at normal incidence; it grows with t, with i and with n.

A thicker slab, a larger angle or a denser glass all increase the shift.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: lateral shift
slides.body_md: A ray meets a glass slab 6.0 cm thick (n = 1.5) at 60°. Find the angle of refraction and the lateral shift.
bullets: Step 1 — $\sin r = \dfrac{\sin 60^\circ}{1.5} = 0.577$, so $r = 35.3^\circ$.
Step 2 — $d = \dfrac{6.0 \times \sin(60^\circ - 35.3^\circ)}{\cos 35.3^\circ} = 3.07$ cm.

The difference i minus r is about twenty four point seven degrees. Six times its sine, divided by the cosine of r, gives a lateral shift of about three point oh eight centimetres. The graph shows the shift rising steeply towards grazing incidence.

slides.heading: Real and apparent depth
slides.body_md:
Rays from O on the floor of a tank bend **away** from the normal at the surface and seem to come from I, nearer the surface. For rays close to the normal ($\tan \approx \sin$):
$$n = \dfrac{\sin r}{\sin i} \approx \dfrac{\tan r}{\tan i} = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}$$
bullets: Water (n = 4/3): a pool looks three quarters as deep as it is.
Viewed obliquely, the bottom looks even shallower.

slides.heading: Apparent shift through a slab or liquid
slides.body_md:
An object seen through a slab of thickness $t$ appears **raised** by
$$s = t - \dfrac{t}{n} = t\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{n}\right)$$
bullets: The shift does not depend on how far the object is below the slab.
Several layers: apparent depth $= \dfrac{t_1}{n_1} + \dfrac{t_2}{n_2} + \dots$
A travelling microscope uses this to measure n: real thickness over apparent thickness.

slides.narration: Put a glass slab on a mark and the mark seems lifted towards you. The slab’s thickness t appears as t over n, so the mark rises by t times one minus one over n. The rise does not depend on how far below the slab the mark is. For several layers, add each thickness over its own index. slides.heading: Worked example 6: a pebble and a stamp
slides.body_md: (a) A pebble lies on the bottom of a pond 40 cm deep (n = 4/3). How deep does it appear from directly above? (b) A stamp is viewed through a glass block 6.0 cm thick (n = 1.5) laid on it. By how much does it appear raised?
bullets: (a) Apparent depth $= \dfrac{40}{4/3} = 30$ cm: the pebble seems 10 cm higher.
(b) $s = t\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{n}\right) = 6.0 \times \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{1.5}\right) = 2.0$ cm.

visual.alt: Worked table: the pebble at 40 centimetres appears at 30 centimetres, raised by 10; the stamp under 6 centimetres of glass appears 4 centimetres below the top, raised by 2

slides.narration: Dividing forty centimetres by four thirds gives thirty, so the pebble looks ten centimetres higher than it is, a real danger for anyone judging a pond’s depth by eye. Through the glass block the stamp seems only four centimetres below the top, so it is raised by six times one third, two centimetres. Notice that water lifts a quarter of the depth, glass a third.

slides.heading: Total internal reflection
slides.body_md: Light going from a **denser** to a **rarer** medium bends away from the normal. As the angle of incidence grows, the refracted ray approaches the surface.
bullets: At the **critical angle C** the refracted ray grazes the surface (angle of refraction 90°).
Beyond C there is no refracted ray: **all** the light is reflected — **total internal reflection** (TIR).
Conditions: light travels from denser to rarer, and meets the boundary at more than C.

slides.narration: Shine light from inside glass towards the air. A ray at a small angle mostly escapes, bending away from the normal. Increase the angle and the escaping ray tilts down towards the surface, until at the critical angle it just skims along it. Beyond that angle nothing escapes, and every bit of the light is reflected back into the glass. This is total internal reflection.

slides.heading: Critical angle and refractive index
slides.body_md:
At $i = C$ the angle of refraction is 90°. For light from a medium of index $n$ into air, Snell’s law gives $n\sin C = 1 \times \sin 90^\circ$:
$$\sin C = \dfrac{1}{n} \qquad\text{(into a medium } n_2 < n_1\text{: } \sin C = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}\text{)}$$
bullets: The larger n, the smaller C: diamond’s small critical angle traps light inside it.

x.label: angle of incidence in the glass (degrees)

visual.alt: Graph of the angle of refraction in air against the angle of incidence inside glass of refractive index 1.5: the refracted angle grows faster than the incident angle and reaches 90 degrees at the critical angle of about 41.8 degrees; beyond it there is no refracted ray
visual.caption: Beyond the critical angle the light is totally reflected.

slides.narration: At the critical angle the refracted ray is at ninety degrees, so Snell’s law gives n times the sine of C equals one. The sine of the critical angle is one over n. If the second medium is not air, it becomes n two over n one. The graph shows the refracted angle in air racing up to ninety degrees as the incident angle in glass reaches about forty two degrees.

slides.heading: Total reflecting prisms
slides.body_md: A glass prism with angles of 45°, 90°, 45° (or 30°, 60°, 90°) reflects light totally where the angle of incidence (45° or 60°) exceeds C (about 42° for glass):
bullets: (a) Ray entering one short face normally: TIR at the hypotenuse, turned through **90°** (periscopes).
(b) Ray entering the hypotenuse normally: two TIRs, turned through **180°** (binoculars, reflectors).
(c) 30°–60°–90° prism: incidence 60° on the hypotenuse is total when n > 1.155; incidence 30° would need n > 2.
Better than silvered mirrors: nearly 100% reflected, no silvering to tarnish, no double images.

slides.narration: A glass prism can act as a perfect mirror. In a right-angled isosceles prism, a ray entering a short face normally meets the long face at forty five degrees, more than the critical angle of glass, and turns through ninety degrees. Enter through the long face instead and it is reflected twice and sent back. In a thirty sixty ninety prism, a sixty degree incidence is also total, but a thirty degree one is not.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: will the prism work under water?
slides.body_md: A right-angled isosceles prism is made of glass with n = 1.45. Does it turn light through 90° by total internal reflection (a) in air, (b) when immersed in water (n = 1.33)?
bullets: (a) $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{1.45}$, so $C = 43.6^\circ$. Incidence at the hypotenuse is $45^\circ > C$: **total** reflection.
(b) $\sin C = \dfrac{1.33}{1.45}$, so $C = 66.5^\circ$. Now $45^\circ < C$: light **leaks** out into the water.

visual.alt: Worked table: in air the critical angle is 43.6 degrees, less than 45, so the light is totally reflected; in water it is 66.5 degrees, more than 45, so light escapes

slides.narration: In air the critical angle of this glass is about forty three point six degrees. The light meets the long face at forty five degrees, just more than that, so it is totally reflected. Put the prism in water and the critical angle depends on the ratio of the two indices, which raises it to about sixty six and a half degrees. Forty five degrees is now too small, and light escapes into the water.

slides.heading: Optical fibres
slides.body_md: A thin glass **core** is surrounded by **cladding** of slightly lower index. Light that meets the core–cladding boundary at more than the critical angle ($\sin C = n_2/n_1$) is totally reflected again and again, and travels along the fibre even round gentle bends.
bullets: Example: core 1.62, cladding 1.52: $C = 69.8^\circ$; rays entering within about 34.1° of the axis are guided.
Uses: telephone and internet cables, endoscopes for seeing inside the body, decorative lamps.
Advantages over copper: huge data capacity, very low loss, no electrical interference.

slides.narration: To sum up: Snell’s law says n sine theta is the same on both sides of a boundary, and the refractive index is c over v. Relative indices are ratios of absolute ones, and their product round a closed set of media is one. A slab shifts a ray sideways without turning it. Depth looks smaller by the factor n. The critical angle has sine one over n, and total internal reflection powers prisms and optical fibres.

sections.heading: 1. Spherical mirrors, R = 2f and the sign convention
sections.body_md:
- **Concave** (converging) and **convex** (diverging) mirrors are parts of a sphere. Pole P, centre of curvature C, radius of curvature R = PC, principal axis through P and C, principal focus F, focal length f = PF. Results hold for **paraxial** rays (close to the axis, small aperture).
- **R = 2f:** a ray parallel to the axis meets the mirror at M; the normal is CM. The angle of incidence θ equals the angle of reflection θ, and ∠MCF = θ (alternate angles), so triangle FCM is isosceles: FC = FM. For a paraxial ray FM ≈ FP, so F is the midpoint of PC and $f = R/2$. The focal length does not depend on the surrounding medium.
- **New Cartesian sign convention** (light drawn from left to right): distances measured from P; along the incident light positive, against it negative; heights above the axis positive. A real object has u < 0; concave mirror f < 0; convex mirror f > 0; a real image (in front) has v < 0, a virtual image (behind) v > 0.

key_terms.definition_md: Rays close to the principal axis and making small angles with it; for them all rays from a point meet at one image point.
The point where rays parallel to the axis meet after reflection (concave mirror) or from which they appear to diverge (convex mirror).

sections.heading: 2. Mirror formula and magnification
sections.body_md:
- **Derivation (concave, object beyond C, real image):** ray AM parallel to the axis reflects through F to A′; ray AP reflects at P to A′. MD is perpendicular to the axis. Triangles A′B′F ~ MDF and A′B′P ~ ABP; with MD = AB and D ≈ P (paraxial): A′B′/AB = B′F/FP = B′P/BP. Putting B′P = −v, BP = −u, FP = −f, B′F = f − v gives $(f - v)/(-f) = v/u$, which rearranges to $\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$.
- **Magnification:** $m = \dfrac{h'}{h} = -\dfrac{v}{u}$. m negative: real, inverted; m positive: virtual, erect; |m| > 1 enlarged.
- **Concave mirror:** object beyond C → image between F and C, smaller; at C → at C, same size; between C and F → beyond C, larger; at F → at infinity; inside F → virtual, erect, enlarged, behind the mirror.
- **Convex mirror:** for every real object the image is virtual, erect, diminished and between P and F (1/v = 1/f − 1/u is a sum of positive terms). Wide field of view: rear-view and security mirrors.
- Method: write u and f with signs, solve for v, then m = −v/u and h′ = mh; interpret the signs.

key_terms.definition_md: Ratio of image height to object height, m = h′/h = −v/u.
An image from which reflected rays only appear to come; it cannot be formed on a screen.

sections.heading: 3. Snell’s law, relative refractive index and slabs
sections.body_md:
- **Laws of refraction:** the incident ray, refracted ray and normal are in one plane; $n_1\sin i = n_2\sin r$ (Snell’s law). Absolute index $n = c/v$. Frequency unchanged; speed and wavelength divided by n.
- **Relative index:** $_1n_2 = \sin i/\sin r = n_2/n_1 = v_1/v_2$; $_2n_1 = 1/{}_1n_2$.
- **Several parallel media:** $n\sin\theta$ is the same in every layer. For a ray going 1 → 2 → 3 → 1: $_1n_2 \times {}_2n_3 \times {}_3n_1 = 1$, so $_2n_3 = {}_1n_3/{}_1n_2$. The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray when the first and last media are the same.
- **Parallel-sided slab:** e = i; **lateral shift** $d = t\sin(i - r)/\cos r$ (zero for normal incidence; increases with t, i and n).

key_terms.definition_md: Speed of light in vacuum divided by its speed in the medium, n = c/v.
Perpendicular distance between the incident ray produced and the emergent ray of a parallel-sided slab.

sections.heading: 4. Real and apparent depth
sections.body_md:
- An object under a liquid seen from above (near-normal rays) appears raised: $n = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}$ (from $n = \sin r/\sin i \approx \tan r/\tan i$).
- **Apparent shift** through a slab or liquid layer of thickness t: $s = t(1 - 1/n)$, independent of the object’s distance below the slab.
- **Several layers:** apparent depth = $t_1/n_1 + t_2/n_2 + \dots$
- Seen obliquely, the bottom looks even shallower. An object in air seen from under water appears **higher** (apparent height = n × real height).
- **Travelling microscope:** n = real thickness ÷ apparent thickness of a slab or liquid.

key_terms.definition_md: The depth at which an object under a refracting medium appears to lie when viewed from above.
The distance an object appears to be raised by a slab or layer: t(1 − 1/n).

sections.heading: 5. Total internal reflection, prisms and fibres
sections.body_md:
- **TIR** happens when light travels from a denser to a rarer medium and meets the boundary at more than the **critical angle** C. At i = C the refracted ray grazes the surface (r = 90°).
- $n\sin C = 1$, so $\sin C = 1/n$; between two media $\sin C = n_2/n_1$ ($n_1 > n_2$). Water 48.8°, crown glass about 41°, diamond 24.4°.
- **Total reflecting prisms:** a 45°–90°–45° glass prism turns a ray through 90° (one TIR at 45°) or 180° (two TIRs, ray entering the hypotenuse); in a 30°–60°–90° prism an incidence of 60° is total for n > 1.155, while 30° would need n > 2. Prisms reflect almost 100%, do not tarnish and give no multiple images. In water the critical angle rises and a prism may stop working.
- **Optical fibre:** glass core (n₁) inside cladding (n₂ < n₁); light meeting the wall at more than C (sin C = n₂/n₁) is guided by repeated TIR. Uses: communication, endoscopy, decorative lamps; low loss, high capacity, no electrical interference.

key_terms.definition_md: Angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction is 90°; sin C = n₂/n₁.
Complete reflection of light at a boundary with a rarer medium when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Mirrors: signs first (u < 0 for a real object; concave f < 0), then 1/v + 1/u = 1/f and m = −v/u; read the nature of the image from the signs.
- Layers: n sin θ is constant; product of relative indices round a closed set of media is 1.
- Apparent depth needs near-normal viewing; shift t(1 − 1/n) is independent of the object’s position.
- TIR: denser to rarer and i > C; compare angles inside the glass with C for the actual surroundings.

questions.stem_md: A convex mirror of focal length 15 cm hangs on the wall of a shop, and a customer stands 2.5 m in front of it. Taking the light from the customer as travelling from left to right (New Cartesian convention), the values to put into the mirror formula are

options.text_md: u = +250 cm and f = +15 cm
u = −250 cm and f = +15 cm
u = −250 cm and f = −15 cm
u = +250 cm and f = −15 cm

questions.solution_md: Distances are measured from the pole. The customer is on the side the light comes from, against the incident light, so u is negative. The focus of a convex mirror lies behind it, along the incident light, so f is positive — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The polished inside of a steel ladle is part of a sphere of radius 9.0 cm. Used as a concave mirror for paraxial rays, the ladle has a focal length of magnitude ___ cm.
questions.solution_md: f = R/2 = 9.0/2 = **4.5** cm (−4.5 cm with the sign of a concave mirror).

questions.stem_md: A jeweller holds a ring 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance v in cm, giving its sign in the New Cartesian convention.
questions.solution_md: $u = -15$ cm, $f = -10$ cm. $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{15} = -\dfrac{1}{30}$, so $v = -30$ cm: a real image 30 cm in front of the mirror.

questions.stem_md: A convex mirror of focal length 30 cm stands on a desk, and a pen is placed 45 cm in front of it. Find the magnification of the image of the pen.
questions.solution_md: $u = -45$ cm, $f = +30$ cm: $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{30} + \dfrac{1}{45} = \dfrac{5}{90}$, so $v = +18$ cm. $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{18}{-45} = 0.40$: erect and diminished.

questions.stem_md: A watch repairer looks at a tiny screw placed 8.0 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 24 cm. The image of the screw is

options.text_md: real and inverted, 12 cm in front of the mirror, 1.5 times the size of the screw
virtual and erect, 12 cm behind the mirror, 1.5 times the size of the screw
virtual and erect, 24 cm behind the mirror, 3 times the size of the screw
real and inverted, 6.0 cm in front of the mirror, 0.75 times the size of the screw

questions.solution_md: $u = -8.0$ cm, $f = -24$ cm: $\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{24} + \dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{2}{24}$, so $v = +12$ cm (behind the mirror, virtual); $m = -\dfrac{12}{-8} = +1.5$ (erect, 1.5 times) — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A concave mirror of focal length 20 cm, lowered into a tank of water, still has a focal length of 20 cm.

**Reason (R):** The focal length of a mirror is half its radius of curvature, and the law of reflection does not involve the refractive index of the surrounding medium.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: reflection obeys i = r in any medium, so the rays meet at the same point, f = R/2, in water as in air — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A spherical mirror forms an image of a real object with a magnification of −0.25. The mirror and its image are

options.text_md: a convex mirror; a virtual, erect image one quarter the size of the object
a concave mirror; a virtual, erect image one quarter the size of the object
a convex mirror; a real, inverted image four times the size of the object
a concave mirror; a real, inverted image one quarter the size of the object

questions.solution_md: m = −v/u is negative, so v has the same sign as u: the image is in front of the mirror, real and inverted. Only a concave mirror forms a real image of a real object, and |m| = 0.25 means one quarter the size — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a laboratory, an object pin stands 36 cm in front of a concave mirror, and a search pin shows no parallax with the inverted image when it is 45 cm in front of the mirror. Find the radius of curvature of the mirror in cm, with its sign.
Using a ray parallel to the principal axis of a concave mirror, prove that its focal length is half its radius of curvature. State the approximation you use.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let a ray parallel to the axis strike the mirror at M. C is the centre of curvature, so CM is the normal at M; call the angle of incidence $\theta$. By the law of reflection the reflected ray MF also makes $\theta$ with CM, so $\angle CMF = \theta$. The incident ray is parallel to the axis, so $\angle MCF = \theta$ (alternate angles). Triangle FCM therefore has two equal angles: $FC = FM$.
For a **paraxial** ray (small aperture) M lies very close to P, so $FM \approx FP$. Then $FC = FP$: F is the midpoint of PC, so $f = PF = \dfrac{PC}{2} = \dfrac{R}{2}$.

questions.solution_md: Isosceles triangle FCM; paraxial FM ≈ FP.

marking_scheme.step: CM is the normal; angles of incidence and reflection both θ
Paraxial rays: FM ≈ FP, so f = R/2

questions.stem_md: Using the mirror formula and the New Cartesian sign convention, show that a real object placed between the pole and the focus of a concave mirror always forms a virtual, erect, magnified image.

answer.model_answer_md: Here $f = -|f|$ and $u = -|u|$ with $|u| < |f|$. Then $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{|u|} - \dfrac{1}{|f|} > 0$, so **v is positive**: the image is behind the mirror, **virtual**. Also $\dfrac{1}{v} < \dfrac{1}{|u|}$, so $v > |u|$ and $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{v}{|u|} > 1$: the image is **erect and magnified**.

marking_scheme.step: v > |u|, so m = v/|u| > 1: erect, magnified

questions.stem_md: A two-wheeler maker proposes fitting plane mirrors instead of convex mirrors as rear-view mirrors, “so that riders judge distances correctly”. Evaluate the proposal.

answer.model_answer_md: A plane mirror shows vehicles at true size, so distances are judged better, but it covers only a **narrow region** behind. A convex mirror gives an **erect, diminished** image of a much **wider field of view**, showing neighbouring lanes. For safety the convex mirror is better, so the proposal should be rejected.

questions.solution_md: Plane: true size, narrow view; convex: wide field of view.

marking_scheme.step: Plane mirror: correct size but a narrow field of view
Convex: erect, wide field of view, so the proposal is less safe

questions.stem_md: Match each mirror set-up in Column A with the image property it relies on, in Column B.

options.text_md: Bulb at the focus of a concave torch reflector
Face held inside the focus of a concave make-up mirror
Convex mirror at a hairpin bend on a hill road
Large concave mirror of a solar cooker

match_right.text_md: Parallel sunlight brought together near the focus
Reflected rays leave parallel, giving a strong beam
An erect, diminished image of a wide stretch of road

questions.solution_md: Torch → parallel beam (1 → r); make-up mirror → erect, enlarged virtual image (2 → p); hill-road mirror → wide view (3 → s); solar cooker → sunlight concentrated near the focus (4 → q).

questions.stem_md: A concave mirror forms a real image exactly the same size as the object when the object is 50 cm in front of it. The focal length of the mirror is

options.text_md: 50 cm
100 cm
25 cm

questions.solution_md: A real image of the same size (m = −1) is formed only when the object is at the centre of curvature, so R = 50 cm and f = R/2 = 25 cm — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? As a candle is moved steadily from far away towards the focus of a concave mirror, its real image moves away from the mirror and grows larger.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. The image moves out from F (object far away) towards infinity (object at F), and |m| = |v/u| grows from nearly zero to very large.

questions.stem_md: The convex rear-view mirror of a scooter has a focal length of 50 cm. A car 1.5 m tall is 4.5 m behind the scooter. Find the height of the car’s image, in cm.

A man wants an upright image of his face 2.5 times life size when he holds a concave shaving mirror 10 cm from his face. Find where the image is formed, and the focal length and radius of curvature the mirror must have.

answer.model_answer_md:
An upright image is virtual, so $m = +2.5 = -\dfrac{v}{u}$ with $u = -10$ cm: $v = -2.5u = +25$ cm, i.e. 25 cm **behind** the mirror.
$\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{25} - \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{2 - 5}{50} = -\dfrac{3}{50}$, so $f = -16.7$ cm.
$R = 2f = -33.3$ cm (the negative signs confirm a concave mirror).

questions.solution_md: m = +2.5 gives v = +25 cm; mirror formula for f; R = 2f.

marking_scheme.step: Erect image: m = +2.5, so v = +25 cm (behind the mirror)

questions.stem_md: A concave mirror is used to throw an image of a small lamp filament, magnified 4 times, onto a wall 3.0 m from the mirror. How far from the mirror must the filament be, and what is the focal length of the mirror?

answer.model_answer_md:
An image on a wall is real and inverted, so $m = -4$ and $v = -300$ cm.
$m = -\dfrac{v}{u}$ gives $u = -\dfrac{v}{m} = -\dfrac{-300}{-4} = -75$ cm: the filament is 75 cm in front of the mirror.
$\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{300} - \dfrac{1}{75} = -\dfrac{5}{300}$, so $f = -60$ cm (focal length 60 cm).

questions.solution_md: Real image: m = −4, v = −300 cm; u = −75 cm; f = −60 cm.

questions.stem_md: A student measures the image distance |v| for several object distances |u| in front of a concave mirror, and plots |v| against |u|. The curve crosses the straight line |v| = |u| at |u| = 30 cm. The focal length of the mirror is

options.text_md: 30 cm
60 cm
15 cm
7.5 cm

questions.solution_md: A real image is as far from the mirror as the object only when both are at the centre of curvature, so R = 30 cm and f = R/2 = 15 cm — option (c).

questions.stem_md: For any real object in front of a convex mirror, the virtual image lies behind the mirror, between its pole and its ___.
questions.solution_md: Between P and the principal **focus**: with f > 0 and u < 0, 1/v = 1/f − 1/u > 1/f, so 0 < v < f.

questions.stem_md: Where must an object be placed in front of a convex mirror of radius of curvature 60 cm so that its image is one quarter of its size? Give u in cm, with its sign.
questions.solution_md: $f = +30$ cm. A convex mirror gives an erect image, so $m = +\dfrac{1}{4} = -\dfrac{v}{u}$, i.e. $v = -\dfrac{u}{4}$. Then $\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{4}{u} + \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{3}{u} = \dfrac{1}{30}$, so $u = -90$ cm (image at $v = +22.5$ cm).

questions.stem_md: An object 5.0 cm tall stands 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Find the height of the image in cm, with its sign.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{20} + \dfrac{1}{30} = -\dfrac{1}{60}$, so $v = -60$ cm; $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -2.0$ and $h' = mh = -10$ cm (real, inverted).

questions.stem_md: A ray travelling in the water of a fish tank (n = 1.33) meets the water–air surface at 30° to the normal. Find the angle of refraction in air, in degrees (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $n_w\sin 30^\circ = 1 \times \sin r$: $\sin r = 1.33 \times 0.500 = 0.665$, so $r = \sin^{-1}(0.665) = 41.7$ degrees (bent away from the normal).

questions.stem_md: Light from a helium–neon laser has a wavelength of 633 nm in air. Find its wavelength in water of refractive index 4/3, in nm (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: The frequency is unchanged and the speed falls by the factor n, so $\lambda_w = \dfrac{\lambda}{n} = \dfrac{633}{4/3} = 475$ nm.

questions.stem_md: The refractive index of water with respect to air is 1.33, and that of a clear acrylic plastic with respect to air is 1.60. The refractive index of the plastic with respect to water is about
questions.solution_md: ${}_wn_p = \dfrac{{}_an_p}{{}_an_w} = \dfrac{1.60}{1.33} \approx 1.20$; 0.83 is the index of water relative to the plastic — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A beam of green light passes from air into a block of acrylic plastic. Which property of the light is the same inside the block as in the air?

options.text_md: its speed
its wavelength
its frequency
its direction, whatever the angle of incidence

questions.solution_md: The frequency is fixed by the source; the speed and the wavelength both fall by the factor n, and the direction changes unless the beam meets the surface normally — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A ray crosses parallel layers from air into oil, from oil into glass and from glass back into air. The product of the three relative refractive indices for these crossings (oil relative to air, glass relative to oil, air relative to glass) equals ___.
questions.solution_md: The product is **1**: each relative index is a ratio of absolute indices, (n_oil/n_air)(n_glass/n_oil)(n_air/n_glass) = 1.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A ray that passes obliquely through a parallel-sided glass slab in air leaves it travelling parallel to its original direction.

**Reason (R):** Glass has a higher refractive index than air, so light travels more slowly in it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R does not explain A. The emergent ray is parallel because the slab’s faces are parallel and the media on both sides are the same, so the refraction at the second face exactly reverses that at the first (sin e = n sin r = sin i) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A ray in air strikes the top of a stack of three parallel transparent layers, glass (n = 1.52), water (n = 1.33) and oil (n = 1.47), at 40° to the normal, and emerges from the bottom of the stack into air. Its angle with the normal after it emerges is

options.text_md: less than 40°, because glass is the densest layer
more than 40°, because the ray last left the oil
about 25°, the angle inside the glass
40°, whatever the refractive indices of the layers

questions.solution_md: At every parallel boundary $n\sin\theta$ is unchanged, so in the final air layer $1 \times \sin\theta = 1 \times \sin 40^\circ$: $\theta = 40^\circ$. (Inside the glass the angle is about $25^\circ$.) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A ray meets a glass block 5.0 cm thick (n = 1.6) at an angle of incidence of 45°. Find the lateral shift of the emergent ray, in cm (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\sin r = \dfrac{\sin 45^\circ}{1.6} = 0.442$, so $r = 26.2^\circ$. $d = \dfrac{t\sin(i - r)}{\cos r} = \dfrac{5.0 \times \sin 18.8^\circ}{\cos 26.2^\circ} = 1.79$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A narrow beam passes obliquely through a parallel-sided glass block. Which one of these changes would REDUCE the lateral shift of the beam?

options.text_md: replacing the block by an equally thick one of lower refractive index
using a thicker block of the same glass
increasing the angle of incidence
replacing the block by an equally thick one of higher refractive index

questions.solution_md: $d = \dfrac{t\sin(i - r)}{\cos r} = t(\sin i - \cos i\tan r)$. A lower n makes r larger (closer to i), so $\tan r$ rises and d falls; a thicker block, a larger i or a higher n all increase d — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A ray passing obliquely from glass (n = 1.5) into water (n = 1.33) bends towards the normal, because water is also denser than air.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. At this boundary the light goes from the optically denser glass into the rarer water, so it bends away from the normal; only the two media at the boundary matter.

questions.stem_md: State the two laws of refraction of light, and define the absolute refractive index of a medium in terms of the speed of light.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal lie in **one plane**. (2) **Snell’s law:** for two given media and colour, sin i / sin r is constant (n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r). **Absolute refractive index:** n = c/v, the speed of light in vacuum over its speed in the medium.

questions.solution_md: Coplanar rays; Snell’s law; n = c/v.

questions.stem_md: A ray passes from medium 1 into medium 2, then into medium 3, and then back into medium 1, the boundaries being parallel. Using Snell’s law at each boundary, prove that 1n2 × 2n3 × 3n1 = 1, and hence express 2n3 in terms of 1n2 and 1n3.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let the angles with the normal be $\theta_1$, $\theta_2$, $\theta_3$ in media 1, 2, 3, and $\theta_1'$ when the ray is back in medium 1. Snell’s law at each boundary: ${}_1n_2 = \dfrac{\sin\theta_1}{\sin\theta_2}$, ${}_2n_3 = \dfrac{\sin\theta_2}{\sin\theta_3}$, ${}_3n_1 = \dfrac{\sin\theta_3}{\sin\theta_1'}$.
Experiment (or the reversibility of light) shows that the ray emerges parallel to the incident ray, $\theta_1' = \theta_1$. Multiplying, every sine cancels: ${}_1n_2\,{}_2n_3\,{}_3n_1 = 1$.
Since ${}_3n_1 = \dfrac{1}{{}_1n_3}$, this gives ${}_2n_3 = \dfrac{{}_1n_3}{{}_1n_2}$.

questions.solution_md: Multiply the three Snell ratios; θ₁′ = θ₁.

marking_scheme.step: Snell’s law written at each of the three boundaries
Emergent ray parallel (θ₁′ = θ₁), so the product is 1

questions.stem_md: Derive an expression for the lateral shift of a ray passing through a parallel-sided slab of thickness t, in terms of t, the angle of incidence i and the angle of refraction r. Evaluate it for t = 3.0 cm, n = √3 and i = 60°.

answer.model_answer_md:
The ray enters at B, travels through the slab to C and leaves parallel to its incident direction. The path inside has length $BC = \dfrac{t}{\cos r}$. The incident ray produced makes an angle $(i - r)$ with BC, so the perpendicular distance from C to it is
$$d = BC\,\sin(i - r) = \dfrac{t\sin(i - r)}{\cos r}$$
Here $\sin r = \dfrac{\sin 60^\circ}{\sqrt 3} = 0.5$, so $r = 30^\circ$ and $d = \dfrac{3.0 \times \sin 30^\circ}{\cos 30^\circ} = 1.73$ cm.

questions.solution_md: BC = t/cos r; d = BC sin(i − r).

marking_scheme.step: Path in the slab t/cos r

questions.stem_md: A ray in water (n = 1.33) meets the flat glass bottom of an aquarium at 40° to the normal and is refracted at 33° inside the glass. Find the refractive index of the glass relative to water, and the absolute refractive index of the glass.

answer.model_answer_md:
${}_wn_g = \dfrac{\sin 40^\circ}{\sin 33^\circ} = \dfrac{0.6428}{0.5446} = 1.18$.
Absolute index: $n_g = n_w \times {}_wn_g = 1.33 \times 1.18 = 1.57$.

questions.solution_md: Ratio of sines; multiply by the index of water.

questions.stem_md: How long does light take to cross a window pane 6.0 mm thick (n = 1.5) at normal incidence? Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and give the answer in picoseconds.
questions.solution_md: Speed in the glass $v = \dfrac{c}{n} = 2.0 \times 10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$, so $t = \dfrac{6.0 \times 10^{-3}}{2.0 \times 10^{8}} = 3.0 \times 10^{-11}$ s, i.e. $3.0 \times 10^{-11} \times 10^{12} = 30$ ps.

questions.stem_md: A coin lies at the bottom of a jar filled with kerosene (n = 1.44) to a depth of 36 cm. How deep does the coin appear when viewed from directly above? Answer in cm.
questions.solution_md: Apparent depth $= \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{n} = \dfrac{36}{1.44} = 25.0$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A printed dot is viewed from above through a glass paperweight 4.5 cm thick (n = 1.5) resting on it. By how much does the dot appear to be raised, in cm?
questions.solution_md: $s = t\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{n}\right) = 4.5 \times \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{1.5}\right) = 1.5$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A glass beaker holds 20 cm of water (n = 4/3) with a 12 cm layer of oil (n = 1.5) floating on it. A scratch on the bottom of the beaker is viewed from directly above. Find its apparent depth below the top surface of the oil, in cm.
questions.solution_md: Each layer looks $t/n$ thick: $\dfrac{20}{4/3} + \dfrac{12}{1.5} = 15 + 8.0 = 23$ cm (the real depth is 32 cm).

questions.stem_md: With a travelling microscope, a mark on the bench is in focus at a scale reading of 4.20 cm. A glass slab is placed on the mark, which is refocused at 5.10 cm; the top surface of the slab is in focus at 7.20 cm. Find the refractive index of the glass (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Real thickness $= 7.20 - 4.20 = 3.00$ cm; apparent thickness $= 7.20 - 5.10 = 2.10$ cm. $n = \dfrac{3.00}{2.10} = 1.43$.

questions.stem_md: A kingfisher hovers 30 cm above the calm surface of a pond. To a fish directly below it, looking up through the water (n = 4/3), the bird appears to be at a height above the surface of

options.text_md: 40 cm
30 cm
70 cm

questions.solution_md: Seen from the denser medium, distances in the rarer medium appear stretched: apparent height = n × real height = (4/3) × 30 = 40 cm, so the bird looks farther away than it is. 22.5 cm divides by n instead of multiplying — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The floor of a swimming pool, seen at a slant from the edge of the pool, appears even shallower than when it is seen from directly above.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. For oblique viewing the rays leaving the water are bent further from the normal, so they trace back to a point even nearer the surface than the near-normal value real depth/n.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The apparent shift of an ink mark seen through a glass slab is the same whether the slab lies on the mark or is held 2 cm above it.

**Reason (R):** The apparent shift produced by a glass slab of thickness t and refractive index n is t/n.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the shift t(1 − 1/n) depends only on the slab, not on where the mark is. R is false: t/n is the apparent thickness of the slab; the shift is t − t/n — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Two identical glass plates, each 3.0 cm thick with refractive index 1.5, are stacked on a printed page. Viewed from directly above, the print appears to be raised by

options.text_md: 1.0 cm
2.0 cm
4.0 cm
3.0 cm

questions.solution_md: The plates act as one slab 6.0 cm thick: $s = 6.0 \times \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{1.5}\right) = 2.0$ cm. 1.0 cm is the shift of one plate; 4.0 cm is the apparent thickness — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A coin lies at the bottom of an empty beaker. Water (n = 4/3) is poured in until the coin, viewed from above, appears to have risen by 2.0 cm. Find the depth of water. What depth of oil (n = 1.5) would give the same rise?

answer.model_answer_md:
Rise $= t\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{n}\right)$. Water: $t\left(1 - \dfrac{3}{4}\right) = \dfrac{t}{4} = 2.0$, so $t = 8.0$ cm.
Oil: $t\left(1 - \dfrac{2}{3}\right) = \dfrac{t}{3} = 2.0$, so $t = 6.0$ cm: less oil is needed because its index is higher.

questions.solution_md: Rise = t(1 − 1/n).

questions.stem_md: A straight stick is dipped obliquely into a pond. Explain why it looks bent at the water surface, and say whether the part under water looks raised or lowered.

answer.model_answer_md: Light from the submerged part bends **away from the normal** on leaving the water, so the eye traces it back to a point **higher** than the real one (apparent depth = real depth ÷ n). Each point is raised in proportion to its depth, so the immersed part looks **raised** and the stick looks bent.

questions.solution_md: Refraction away from the normal raises each point by depth × (1 − 1/n).

marking_scheme.step: Rays bend away from the normal on leaving the water
Each point appears raised (more for deeper points): stick looks bent upwards

questions.stem_md: With a ray diagram described in words, show that for an object at the bottom of a liquid of refractive index n, viewed from directly above, n = real depth ÷ apparent depth. State the approximation you make.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let O be the object at depth OB below the point B of the surface directly above it. A ray OB along the normal passes straight out. A second ray OA meets the surface at A at a small angle $i$ and refracts away from the normal at angle $r$; produced backwards it meets the normal BO at I, the image. Then $\tan i = \dfrac{AB}{OB}$ and $\tan r = \dfrac{AB}{IB}$.
Snell’s law at A (liquid to air): $n = \dfrac{\sin r}{\sin i}$. For near-normal viewing, i and r are **small**, so $\sin \approx \tan$:
$$n \approx \dfrac{\tan r}{\tan i} = \dfrac{OB}{IB} = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}$$

questions.solution_md: Small angles: sin ≈ tan.

marking_scheme.step: Diagram: normal ray and an oblique ray traced back to I
tan i = AB/OB, tan r = AB/IB; n = sin r/sin i

questions.stem_md: A glass block 6.0 cm thick (n = 1.5) lies on the bottom of a tank, with a scratch on the tank floor beneath it, and is covered by 16 cm of water (n = 4/3). Viewed from directly above, find the apparent depth of the scratch below the water surface and how far it appears to be raised.

answer.model_answer_md:
Viewed from above, each layer appears $t/n$ thick.
Water: $\dfrac{16}{4/3} = 12$ cm. Glass: $\dfrac{6.0}{1.5} = 4.0$ cm.
Apparent depth $= 12 + 4.0 = 16$ cm, while the real depth is $16 + 6.0 = 22$ cm, so the scratch appears raised by $6.0$ cm (4.0 cm by the water and 2.0 cm by the glass).

questions.solution_md: Sum of t/n over the layers.

marking_scheme.step: Glass appears 4.0 cm; apparent depth 16 cm

questions.stem_md: Find the critical angle for light travelling from dense flint glass (n = 1.72) into air, in degrees (3 significant figures).
A block of crown glass (n = 1.52) is in contact with glycerine (n = 1.47). Find the critical angle for light travelling in the glass towards the glycerine, in degrees (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\sin C = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \dfrac{1.47}{1.52} = 0.9671$, so $C = \sin^{-1}(0.9671) = 75.3$ degrees: only rays meeting the boundary almost at grazing incidence are totally reflected.

questions.stem_md: Light travels at 1.8 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a certain plastic. The critical angle for light passing from this plastic into air is about
questions.solution_md: $n = \dfrac{c}{v} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{1.8 \times 10^{8}} = 1.67$, so $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{n} = 0.60$ and $C \approx 36.9^\circ$; 53° is the angle whose cosine is 0.60 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A right-angled isosceles prism for a toy periscope is moulded from a plastic of refractive index 1.40. A ray entering one short face normally meets the long face at 45°. At the long face the light

options.text_md: is totally reflected, because 45° is more than the critical angle of about 44.4°
is totally reflected, because every ray inside a prism is reflected at its long face
passes straight through without bending, because it entered the prism normally
is partly refracted out, because 45° is less than the critical angle of about 45.6°

questions.solution_md: $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{1.40}$, so $C \approx 45.6^\circ$. The angle of incidence, 45°, is just below C, so total internal reflection does not occur; some light escapes and the periscope image is dim — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A glass prism (n = 1.5) has angles of 30°, 60° and 90°. A ray enters the shorter of the two faces that meet at the right angle, normally, and then meets the hypotenuse face. The angle of incidence at the hypotenuse, and what happens there, are

options.text_md: 60°; the light is totally reflected, since the critical angle of the glass is about 41.8°
30°; the light is totally reflected, since 30° exceeds the critical angle of the glass
30°; the light is refracted out of the hypotenuse face
60°; the light is refracted out, since the critical angle of the glass is about 62°

questions.solution_md: The shorter leg is opposite the 30° angle. A ray entering it normally travels parallel to the longer leg and meets the hypotenuse at 60° (the angle between the hypotenuse’s normal and the longer leg). Since sin C = 1/1.5 gives C ≈ 41.8° < 60°, the light is totally reflected — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A ray enters one face of an equilateral glass prism (n = 1.5) normally. It meets the second face at an angle of incidence of 60°, is totally reflected there, and then leaves through the third face. Through what angle has the ray been turned in all?
questions.solution_md: Reflection at an angle of incidence of 60° turns a ray through 180° − 2 × 60° = 60°. The reflected ray then meets the third face normally (by symmetry), so it leaves without further bending: the total deviation is 60° — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A ray travelling inside a block of ice (n = 1.31) that meets the ice–air surface at 52° to the normal is totally reflected.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. sin C = 1/1.31, so C ≈ 49.8°; the angle of incidence, 52°, exceeds C, and the light is going from the denser ice to the rarer air, so it is totally reflected.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A right-angled isosceles glass prism (n = 1.5) can send a beam of light back parallel to its original direction.

**Reason (R):** A beam entering the hypotenuse face normally meets each of the two shorter faces at 45°, which is more than the critical angle of the glass, so it is totally reflected twice.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: the two total internal reflections at 45° each turn the beam through 90°, so it leaves through the hypotenuse reversed, turned through 180° — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Light can be guided along an optical fibre whose cladding has a higher refractive index than its core.

**Reason (R):** Total internal reflection can occur only when light travelling in an optically denser medium meets a boundary with a rarer one.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: with a cladding of higher index, light in the core meets a denser medium, so it is never totally reflected and leaks out into the cladding — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A small lamp lies at the bottom of an ornamental pool, 60 cm below the surface (n of water = 4/3). Explain why light from the lamp leaves the surface only through a circular patch, and find the radius of the patch.

answer.model_answer_md:
Rays from the lamp that meet the surface at more than the critical angle C are **totally reflected** back into the water; only rays within C of the vertical escape. They meet the surface inside a circle centred above the lamp, whose edge is where $i = C$.
$\sin C = \dfrac{1}{n} = \dfrac{3}{4}$, so $C = 48.6^\circ$.
Radius $r = h\tan C = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{n^2 - 1}} = 60 \times 1.13 = 68.0$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Only rays within C escape; r = h tan C.

marking_scheme.step: Rays beyond C are totally reflected; the edge of the patch is at i = C

questions.stem_md: Define the critical angle for light passing from a denser medium (index n₁) into a rarer one (index n₂), and obtain the relation between the critical angle and the two refractive indices.

answer.model_answer_md: The critical angle C is the **angle of incidence in the denser medium** for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is **90°** (the refracted ray grazes the boundary). Applying Snell’s law at that angle: $n_1\sin C = n_2\sin 90^\circ = n_2$, so $\sin C = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}$; for the rarer medium air, $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{n}$.

questions.solution_md: Snell’s law with r = 90°.

marking_scheme.step: Definition: angle of incidence in the denser medium giving r = 90°
n₁ sin C = n₂, so sin C = n₂/n₁

questions.stem_md: Describe, with ray paths described in words, how a right-angled isosceles glass prism can be used (i) to turn a ray through 90°, and (ii) to turn it through 180°. State the angle of incidence at each reflecting face, and why the reflection there is total.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) The ray enters one of the shorter faces **normally**, passes straight in and meets the hypotenuse face at **45°**; it is totally reflected and leaves normally through the other short face, turned through **90°**. (ii) The ray enters the **hypotenuse** face normally, meets each shorter face in turn at **45°**, is totally reflected at both, and leaves through the hypotenuse, turned through **180°**. The reflection is total because the light goes from glass to air and 45° exceeds the critical angle of glass, about 42°.

questions.solution_md: 45° incidence exceeds C ≈ 42° for glass.

marking_scheme.step: 90° prism path with one TIR at 45°
180° prism path with two TIRs at 45°

questions.stem_md: Describe the construction of an optical fibre and explain how light travels along it, even when the fibre is gently bent. Give two uses of optical fibres.

answer.model_answer_md: An optical fibre has a very thin glass or plastic **core**, surrounded by a **cladding** of slightly lower refractive index and a protective outer coat. Light entering one end close to the axis meets the core–cladding boundary at an angle **greater than the critical angle**, so it is **totally reflected**, again and again, with almost no loss. A gentle bend keeps the angle of incidence above the critical angle, so the light follows the fibre. Uses: telephone and internet cables; endoscopes for viewing inside the body.

questions.solution_md: Core of higher index inside cladding; repeated TIR.

marking_scheme.step: Core inside cladding of lower refractive index
Repeated TIR at angles above C, also round gentle bends

questions.stem_md: An optical fibre has a core of refractive index 1.50 and cladding of refractive index 1.45. Find the largest angle to the fibre axis at which a ray in air can enter the flat end of the core and still be totally reflected at the core–cladding boundary, in degrees (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: At the wall: $\sin C = \dfrac{1.45}{1.50}$, so $C = 75.16^\circ$; inside the core the ray may make at most $90^\circ - C = 14.8^\circ$ with the axis. At the end face: $\sin\theta = 1.50\sin 14.8^\circ = 0.384$, so $\theta = \sin^{-1}(0.384) = 22.6$ degrees (equivalently $\sin\theta = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2}$).

marking_scheme.step: C ≈ 75.2°, so at most 14.8° to the axis inside

questions.stem_md: A jeweller claims that a small right-angled isosceles prism cut from diamond (n = 2.42) will still turn light through 90° by total internal reflection when it is used under water (n = 1.33), although a glass prism (n = 1.5) would not. Evaluate the claim.

answer.model_answer_md: The claim is **correct**. In water, diamond: $\sin C = \dfrac{1.33}{2.42}$, $C \approx 33.3^\circ$, less than the 45° angle of incidence, so the light is totally reflected. Glass: $\sin C = \dfrac{1.33}{1.5}$, $C \approx 62.5^\circ$, more than 45°, so light leaks out into the water.

questions.solution_md: Compare 45° with sin⁻¹(1.33/n).

marking_scheme.step: Diamond in water: C ≈ 33° < 45°, total reflection
Glass in water: C ≈ 62° > 45°, fails: claim correct

questions.stem_md: Light starts to leak out of an optical fibre at a place where the fibre is bent very sharply. This is because at the bend

options.text_md: rays meet the core–cladding boundary at less than the critical angle
the refractive index of the core rises above that of the cladding
the light slows down and its frequency falls
the cladding absorbs all the light that reaches it

questions.solution_md: At a sharp bend the core wall turns towards the rays, so they strike it more nearly head-on; the angle of incidence falls below the critical angle and part of the light is refracted out of the core — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Match each boundary in Column A, crossed by light going from the first medium into the second, with its critical angle in Column B.

options.text_md: Water (n = 1.33) to air
Crown glass (n = 1.52) to air
Sapphire (n = 1.77) to air
Crown glass (n = 1.52) to water (n = 1.33)

questions.solution_md: sin C = n₂/n₁: water–air 48.8° (1 → s); glass–air 41.1° (2 → q); sapphire–air 34.4° (3 → p); glass–water 61.0° (4 → r).

questions.stem_md: (a) With a labelled ray diagram described in words, derive the mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f for a concave mirror forming a real image of an object placed beyond its centre of curvature, using the New Cartesian sign convention. [3] (b) An object 4.0 cm tall is placed 25 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Find the position, size and nature of the image. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Object AB stands on the axis beyond C. Ray AM, parallel to the axis, reflects through F; ray AP, to the pole, reflects at an equal angle. They meet at A′, and A′B′ is the real, inverted image between C and F. Draw MD perpendicular to the axis.
Triangles A′B′F and MDF are similar: $\dfrac{A'B'}{MD} = \dfrac{B'F}{FD}$. Triangles A′B′P and ABP are similar: $\dfrac{A'B'}{AB} = \dfrac{B'P}{BP}$. For a small aperture $MD = AB$ and $D \approx P$, so $\dfrac{B'F}{FP} = \dfrac{B'P}{BP}$.
With the signs $B'P = -v$, $BP = -u$, $FP = -f$, $B'F = f - v$: $\dfrac{f - v}{-f} = \dfrac{v}{u}$, so $uv - uf = vf$; dividing by $uvf$: $\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$.

(b) $u = -25$ cm, $f = -20$ cm: $\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{20} + \dfrac{1}{25} = -\dfrac{1}{100}$, so $v = -100$ cm. $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -4.0$, so $h' = -16$ cm: real, inverted, four times enlarged, 100 cm in front of the mirror.

questions.solution_md: Two pairs of similar triangles with paraxial approximation; then signs.

marking_scheme.step: Ray diagram: rays via F and P, MD drawn
Similar triangles with MD = AB, D ≈ P
m = −4; image 16 cm tall, real, inverted

questions.stem_md: (a) Using the mirror formula and the New Cartesian sign convention, show that a convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image of a real object, lying between its pole and its focus. [2] (b) Give one reason why a convex mirror is used as a rear-view mirror and one reason why a concave mirror is used in a torch. [1] (c) A convex mirror of focal length 20 cm forms an image one fifth the size of an object. Find the object distance and the image distance. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) For a convex mirror $f > 0$; a real object has $u < 0$. Then $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{|u|}$, which is positive and larger than $\dfrac{1}{f}$: so $0 < v < f$, the image is behind the mirror (**virtual**) between P and F. Also $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{v}{|u|}$ is positive (**erect**) and, since $v < f$ and $\dfrac{1}{v} > \dfrac{1}{|u|}$, $v < |u|$, so $m < 1$ (**diminished**).

(b) Rear-view: it gives an erect image of a wide field of view. Torch: a bulb at the focus of a concave reflector gives a parallel beam.

(c) Erect image: $m = +\dfrac{1}{5} = -\dfrac{v}{u}$, so $v = -\dfrac{u}{5}$. Then $-\dfrac{5}{u} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{20}$, so $-\dfrac{4}{u} = \dfrac{1}{20}$: $u = -80$ cm and $v = +16$ cm (16 cm behind the mirror).

questions.stem_md: (a) State Snell’s law. Show that a ray passing obliquely through a parallel-sided glass slab in air emerges parallel to its original direction. [2] (b) A ray in air falls at 50° on a glass slab 4.0 cm thick of refractive index 1.55. Find the angle of refraction and the lateral shift of the emergent ray. [2] (c) A mark on the lower face of the same slab is viewed from directly above. By how much does it appear to be raised? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Snell’s law: $n_1\sin i = n_2\sin r$ (with the incident ray, refracted ray and normal in one plane). At the top face $\sin i = n\sin r$. The faces are parallel, so the ray meets the lower face at $r$; there $n\sin r = \sin e$. Hence $\sin e = \sin i$, $e = i$: the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray (only shifted sideways).

(b) $\sin r = \dfrac{\sin 50^\circ}{1.55} = 0.494$, so $r = 29.6^\circ$. $d = \dfrac{t\sin(i - r)}{\cos r} = \dfrac{4.0 \times \sin 20.4^\circ}{\cos 29.6^\circ} = 1.60$ cm.

(c) $s = t\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{n}\right) = 4.0 \times \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{1.55}\right) = 1.42$ cm.

questions.solution_md: e = i at parallel faces; d = t sin(i − r)/cos r; s = t(1 − 1/n).

marking_scheme.step: sin e = n sin r = sin i, so e = i

questions.stem_md: (a) What is meant by the critical angle? Derive the relation between the critical angle and the refractive index of a medium surrounded by air. [2] (b) An optical fibre has a core of refractive index 1.58 and cladding of refractive index 1.50. Find (i) the critical angle at the core–cladding boundary, (ii) the largest angle a ray inside the core may make with the fibre axis and still be guided along it. [2] (c) Give one advantage of optical fibres over copper cables for carrying signals. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The critical angle is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is 90°. Snell’s law from the medium (index n) into air at that angle: $n\sin C = 1 \times \sin 90^\circ$, so $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{n}$.

(b)(i) $\sin C = \dfrac{1.50}{1.58} = 0.9494$, so $C = 71.7^\circ$.
(ii) The ray meets the wall at $90^\circ - \theta$ when it makes $\theta$ with the axis; it is guided while $90^\circ - \theta > C$, i.e. $\theta < 90^\circ - 71.7^\circ = 18.3^\circ$.

(c) Any one: far greater information capacity; very low loss over long distances; no electrical interference or cross-talk; lighter and thinner.

questions.solution_md: sin C = 1/n; sin C = n₂/n₁ for the fibre; θ < 90° − C.

marking_scheme.step: n sin C = 1, so sin C = 1/n

questions.stem_md: (a) Describe, with the ray path described in words, how a right-angled isosceles glass prism turns a ray through 180°, giving the angle of incidence at each face. [2] (b) Find the least refractive index the prism material must have for it to work in air. [1] (c) A 30°–60°–90° prism of glass with n = 1.50 is set so that a ray entering its shorter right-angle face normally meets the hypotenuse at 60°. Show whether the ray is totally reflected there (i) in air, (ii) when the prism is immersed in water (n = 1.33). [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The ray enters the hypotenuse face normally (angle of incidence 0°, no bending), meets one shorter face at 45° and is totally reflected, travels parallel to the hypotenuse, meets the other shorter face at 45° and is totally reflected again, then leaves the hypotenuse face normally, travelling back parallel to its original path.

(b) Total reflection at 45° needs $45^\circ > C$, i.e. $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{n} < \sin 45^\circ$: $n > \sqrt 2 = 1.41$.

(c)(i) In air $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{1.50}$, $C = 41.8^\circ < 60^\circ$: **totally reflected**.
(ii) In water $\sin C = \dfrac{1.33}{1.50}$, $C = 62.5^\circ > 60^\circ$: **not** totally reflected; part of the light escapes into the water.

questions.solution_md: Two TIRs at 45°; n > √2; compare 60° with C in air and in water.
